analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off the Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina coasts through 2032.
analysis.headline: The drilling ban never got a vote: after introduction it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend the existing ban on offshore oil and gas drilling in the eastern Gulf of Mexico from 2022 through June 2032, and add new bans covering the South Atlantic planning area and the Straits of Florida. That covers federal waters off the coasts of Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina. Existing leases would be untouched, and drilling for environmental restoration projects like beach nourishment would still be allowed. The bill was introduced in January 2023 by Rep. Michael Waltz, referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then to its Energy and Minerals subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and local economies of Gulf and South Atlantic coastal states, whose beaches, fisheries, and tourism businesses are shielded from new offshore drilling and the risk of spills. In 2010 the Deepwater Horizon spill in the Gulf devastated Gulf Coast tourism and fishing for months; this bill would lock in the protection that coastal-state politicians of both parties have sought since then.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal residents, tourism, and fishing communities

how_it_helps.text: Extends the eastern Gulf of Mexico drilling moratorium from June 30, 2022 to June 30, 2032, keeping the military testing ranges and tourist beaches off Florida's Gulf Coast closed to new drilling.
Adds the South Atlantic Planning Area and the Straits of Florida Planning Area to the moratorium, closing federal waters off Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina to new oil and gas leases.
Preserves existing valid leases, so the ban is a forward-looking protection rather than a confiscation of current production.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would be shut out of new federal leasing in the covered waters through 2032. The federal government would forgo any lease-sale revenue from those areas, and the country would forgo whatever recoverable oil and gas lies there. Existing leases are grandfathered, so no current production is taken away.

drawbacks.text: The bill forecloses domestic energy development in a large area of federal waters, forgoing lease revenue for the Treasury and potential energy supply at a time when expanded production is often cited as a goal.
A statutory moratorium is only as durable as Congress chooses to make it; a future Congress could amend or repeal it, so it is protection on paper rather than permanently.
Because existing leases are exempt, drilling could still occur in the covered waters wherever a lease predates enactment, so the protection is incomplete even for supporters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the coastal states covered, the bill offers substantial protection of tourism, fishing, and beach economies against spill risk, at the cost of forgone energy development in federal waters and any associated federal revenue. The production cost is speculative and deferred, while spill damage to coastal economies is concrete and proven — Deepwater Horizon being the standard example. The main weakness is that it is region-specific rather than a national offshore policy, and it leaves existing leases untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, then sent to the Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee three weeks later, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Waltz introduced the bill on January 26, 2023 with ten Republican cosponsors from Florida and South Carolina, all members whose districts and states border the protected waters.
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day; that committee was the sole committee of referral.
On February 21, 2023 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, which is where the action history ends.
No further action was taken through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, so the moratorium extension was never debated or voted on in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas producers, who remain able to seek leases in the South Atlantic and Straits of Florida areas the bill would have closed, since no competing protection was enacted either. Coastal communities got nothing, but also lost nothing they already had.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore drillers and the committee status quo

for.name: Rep. Michael Waltz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend and expand the offshore drilling moratorium off Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina.

for.name: 10 of 224 House Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors, all from Florida and South Carolina coastal districts

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, which sat in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All eleven sponsors were House Republicans from Florida and South Carolina, but because the bill never reached a hearing, markup, or vote, no record exists of broader support or opposition on either side.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from new federal leases in the eastern Gulf, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida through 2032, closing off acreage they otherwise could bid on. Their interest in keeping those waters open runs against the coastal tourism and fishing economies that depend on spill-free waters.

industries.industry: Gulf and South Atlantic coastal tourism and recreation
industries.note: Beach economies from Florida's Gulf Coast to the Carolinas would keep new drilling off their shores through 2032, protecting the natural asset their businesses sell. The 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill showed how quickly those economies collapse when oil reaches shore.
Fisheries in the covered waters would be spared new drilling activity and spill risk, protecting both the resource and the fishing livelihoods that depend on it.
